body:
This post becomes much less confusing when I replace the first sentence's "pointer capture" with "pointer lock" :). Let me edit the OP.

If I am understanding pointer capture correctly, it allows you to specify an element that intercepts all pointer events (for a specific pointer) with no restrictions? Wow, interesting. Do you have a quick sample of code that uses it in a "good" way (e.g. to implement the volume slider example from [the spec](https://w3c.github.io/pointerevents/#dfn-pointer-capture))?

If that is indeed how it works, it does seem like the kind of powerful feature that should get restricted. We have several such restriction models to my knowledge:

- Sandbox flags: allowed in unsandboxed iframes; disallowed in sandboxed iframes, but with an opt-in to re-allow it. (Your proposal)
- Feature policy (new hotness)/allow* attributes (old workhorse): disallowed in (cross-origin? https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2184) iframes by default; opt-in to re-allow.
- Secure contexts only: orthogonal to the above, but maybe also worth considering.
- CSP: this feels less applicable, but I'm not too knowledgeable in this area.
- X-IFrame-Options, rel=noopener: also not applicable, and somewhat legacy I believe?

What are your thoughts, especially on sandboxing vs. feature policy? Do you think the analogy to Pointer Lock is strong enough that sandboxing is the clear winner? I don't really know myself.

/cc @mikewest

> This post becomes much less confusing when I replace the first sentence's "pointer capture" with "pointer lock" :). Let me edit the OP.

Damn, sorry - was rushing.  Thanks.

>  Do you have a quick sample of code that uses it in a "good" way (e.g. to implement the volume slider example from the spec)?

There's a simple demo [here](https://patrickhlauke.github.io/touch/tests/pointercapture.html) but it's not very real world.  As a very real-world example use case, pan [an embedded google map](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/examples/map-simple) and let your mouse cursor leave the bounds of the iframe.  The Google Maps folks say it's really important to their user experience that the map continues to pan when the cursor is outside the frame, but this works in Chrome today only due to a [non-standard quirk in blink/WebKit](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=269917).

> What are your thoughts, especially on sandboxing vs. feature policy? 

AFAIK @clelland is specing feature policy in a way that lets us redefine the existing iframe attributes like `allow-pointer-lock` in terms of a feature policy.  I assume we'd want to do the same for pointer capture?  Ian do we need to block on any FP spec work, or can we just copy the existing pattern for pointer lock and "upgrade" them to FP together?

> AFAIK @clelland is specing feature policy in a way that lets us redefine the existing iframe attributes like allow-pointer-lock in terms of a feature policy.

My understanding is that feature policy is meant to subsume the allow* attributes (currently allowfullscreen, allowusermedia, and allowpaymentrequest), but it is not meant to subsume the sandbox flags. The models seem fundamentally different: feature policy is featurewise-opt-in, whereas sandbox is mass-opt-out-plus-featurewise-opt-back-in. I could be wrong though; maybe @clelland has a way of reconciling them. Looking forward to hearing his thoughts.

Oh I'm sorry - yes I was getting those confused.  Let's see what Ian has to say.

And now that I've filed some bugs for this, there's more discussion on the [PEWG issue](https://github.com/w3c/pointerevents/issues/16) around avoiding the need for it.  So let's see where that goes.

Oops -- dropped this for a year :(

My feeling on this is that almost all of the existing sandbox attributes could have been implemented as policy-controlled features. If I were writing sandbox today, I would probably just use the `sandbox` attribute to isolate the frame with a unique opaque origin, and to have that turn a set of features off, but let feature policy be the way to re-enable them within that frame.

(I wrote [Migrating Sandbox attributes to Feature Policy](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KsCFmugEAZf1LT_C3ZCj8FfkkljZV3D3EoMenX7yQto/edit#heading=h.ob81ggvog3md) last year to explore the possibility of doing just this)

I don't think that @domenic's point about opt-out vs opt-in represents a fundamental difference -- it would mean that the sandbox attribute would have to be defined as disabling a specific set of features which are normally enabled in cross-origin frames.

If we were to do this, it would mean that all of those features would be disabled in sandboxed frames, just as they are today, but that authors could just as easily choose to disable them in any other frame, with or without sandboxing.

Going forward, It looks like most "powerful" features are already being disabled in cross-origin frames by default. This works perfectly with feature policy, and still integrates with sandbox:

    <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" allow="payment"></iframe>

should work to enable PaymentRequest in an otherwise sandboxed frame, for instance. We could easily do the same thing with a feature named `pointer-capture`.
